The intersection of a random plane conic \(Q\) with the smooth cubic \(C\) has degree  

\[
\deg C\cdot \deg Q = 3\cdot 2 = 6 .
\]

For a conic that meets \(C\) transversely the six intersection points are distinct.  
Let  

\[
\mathcal Q_p=\{ \text{non‑zero quadratic forms in }x,y,z\}/\mathbb F_p^\times ,
\qquad |\mathcal Q_p| = \frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For a fixed \(\mathbb F_p\)-rational point \(P\in C(\mathbb F_p)\) the condition “\(P\in Q\)” is a single linear equation on the six coefficients of the quadratic form, so the subspace of forms vanishing at \(P\) has dimension \(5\). Hence the number of conics containing \(P\) is  

\[
\frac{p^{5}-1}{p-1}=p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr(P\in Q)=\frac{p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}{p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}
          = \frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

Let \(N_p(Q)\) be the number of \(\mathbb F_p\)-points of \(C\cap Q\).  
By linearity of expectation,

\[
\mathbb E[N_p]=\sum_{P\in C(\mathbb F_p)}\Pr(P\in Q)
            = |C(\mathbb F_p)|\;\Pr(P\in Q).
\]

For a smooth cubic (genus 1) the Hasse–Weil bound gives  

\[
|C(\mathbb F_p)| = p+1-a_p,\qquad |a_p|\le 2\sqrt p .
\]

Hence  

\[
\mathbb E[N_p]=\frac{p+1-a_p}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)
              = 1 + O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\right).
\]

The restriction to transverse conics removes only those conics that are tangent at a point of \(C\); the tangency condition imposes an extra linear equation, so the proportion of such conics is \(O(1/p)\) and does not affect the limit.

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=\lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb E[N_p]=1 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places, the limiting value is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}

The cubic \(C\) is smooth, and the point  

\[
P=(1:0:-1)
\]

lies on \(C\) because \(1^{3}+0^{3}+(-1)^{3}=0\).  
The tangent line to \(C\) at a point \((x:y:z)\) is given by  

\[
3x^{2}(X-x)+3y^{2}(Y-y)+3z^{2}(Z-z)=0 .
\]

At \(P\) this yields \(x+z=0\); this line is a flex (inflection) line, so it meets \(C\) with multiplicity 3 at \(P\).

All lines through \(P\) have the form  

\[
\ell_{t} :\; y = t\,(x+z),\qquad t\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\},
\]

where \(t=\infty\) corresponds to the flex line \(x+z=0\).

Parametrize \(\ell_{t}\) by  
\[
( x , y , z ) = (1,\;\lambda t,\; -1+\lambda),\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb{C},
\]
so that \(\lambda=0\) gives the point \(P\).  
Substituting into the cubic equation \(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=0\) gives  

\[
1+(\lambda t)^{3}+(-1+\lambda)^{3}=0
\Longrightarrow 
\lambda\bigl[\lambda^{2}(t^{3}+1)-3\lambda+3\bigr]=0 .
\]

Hence the other two intersection points of \(\ell_{t}\) with \(C\) are the roots of  

\[
\lambda^{2}(t^{3}+1)-3\lambda+3=0 .
\]

The line \(\ell_{t}\) is tangent to \(C\) at a point distinct from \(P\) precisely when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
\Delta = (-3)^{2}-4\cdot 3\,(t^{3}+1)=9-12(t^{3}+1)=0
\Longrightarrow t^{3}=-\frac14 .
\]

The equation \(t^{3}=-\frac14\) has three distinct complex solutions, giving three distinct lines \(\ell_{t}\) (each tangent to \(C\) at a point different from \(P\)).

Together with the flex line \(x+z=0\) (the tangent at \(P\) itself), there are

\[
1 \text{ (flex line)} + 3 \text{ (other tangents)} = 4
\]

distinct projective lines through \(P\) that are tangent to the cubic \(C\).

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

For a line \(\ell\) through  

\[
P=(1:0:-1)
\]

write its linear equation as  

\[
\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=0 ,\qquad \alpha-\gamma =0 .
\]

Hence we may set \(\alpha=\gamma\) and obtain the one‑parameter family  

\[
\ell_\lambda:\;x+z+\lambda y =0 ,\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\},
\]

where \(\lambda=\infty\) corresponds to the line \(y=0\).

---

On \(\ell_\lambda\) we have \(z=-x-\lambda y\). Substituting in  

\[
F(x,y,z)=x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=0
\]

gives  

\[
x^{3}+y^{3}+(-x-\lambda y)^{3}=0 .
\]

If \(y\neq 0\) put \(t=x/y\); then  

\[
t^{3}+1+(-t-\lambda)^{3}=0
\]

which simplifies to  

\[
-3\lambda t^{2}-3\lambda^{2}t+(1-\lambda^{3})=0 .
\]

For \(\lambda\neq 0\) this is a quadratic in \(t\); the third intersection point is the
fixed point \(P\) (corresponding to \(y=0\)).  
A line is tangent to \(C\) exactly when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. its
discriminant vanishes.

---

### Discriminant condition

The quadratic can be written as  

\[
a t^{2}+b t+c=0,\qquad a=3\lambda,\; b=3\lambda^{2},\; c=\lambda^{3}-1 .
\]

Its discriminant is  

\[
\Delta=b^{2}-4ac
      =9\lambda^{4}-12\lambda(\lambda^{3}-1)
      =3\lambda\,(4-\lambda^{3}) .
\]

Thus \(\Delta=0\) iff  

\[
\lambda =0\quad\text{or}\quad \lambda^{3}=4 .
\]

* \(\lambda =0\) gives the line \(x+z=0\), which is the tangent at \(P\); in fact
\(P\) is an inflection point, so the intersection multiplicity there is \(3\).

* \(\lambda^{3}=4\) yields three distinct values  

\[
\lambda = 4^{1/3},\; 4^{1/3}\,\omega,\; 4^{1/3}\,\omega^{2},
\qquad \omega^{3}=1,
\]

each giving a line that meets \(C\) at \(P\) (simple intersection) and is tangent
to \(C\) at another point.

The remaining line \(y=0\) (\(\lambda=\infty\)) meets the cubic transversely at three
distinct points, so it is **not** tangent.

---

Hence the lines through \(P\) that are tangent to \(C\) are:

* the inflection tangent \(x+z=0\);
* the three lines corresponding to the three cube‑roots of \(4\).

That makes a total of \(1+3=4\) distinct projective lines.

\[

\[

\[

\[

A line is tangent to the cubic at a point with \(y\neq0\) precisely when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. its discriminant vanishes:

\[

\mu^{3}x^{3}-\lambda^{3}(x+z)^{3}+\mu^{3}z^{3}=0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Writing \(t=x/z\) (so \(z\neq0\)) gives the cubic equation  

\[
H(t)=\mu^{3}t^{3}-\lambda^{3}(t+1)^{3}+\mu^{3}=0 .
\]

Because the line passes through \(P\) we have the factor \(t+1\); factoring yields  

\[
H(t)=(t+1)\bigl[(\mu^{3}-\lambda^{3})t^{2}+(-2\lambda^{3}-\mu^{3})t+(\mu^{3}-\lambda^{3})\bigr].
\]

The line \(\ell_{\lambda,\mu}\) is tangent to \(C\) at a point distinct from \(P\) exactly when the quadratic factor has a double root, i.e. when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
\Delta = (-2\lambda^{3}-\mu^{3})^{2}-4(\mu^{3}-\lambda^{3})^{2}
      = 3\mu^{3}\bigl(4\lambda^{3}-\mu^{3}\bigr)=0 .
\]

Thus either \(\mu=0\) (the tangent at \(P\)) or  

\[
4\lambda^{3}=\mu^{3}.
\]

The latter equation has three solutions for the ratio \(\mu/\lambda\) (the three cube‑roots of \(4\)). Hence there are **three** lines through \(P\) that are tangent to \(C\) at a point different from \(P\).

Including the tangent line at \(P\) itself, the total number of distinct projective lines through \(P\) that are tangent to the cubic is  

\[
1+3 = 4 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places, the answer is  

\[
\boxed{4.0000}

\[
\ell\cdot C = P+Q_{1}+Q_{2},
\]

\[

\]

\[
2g-2 = d\,(2\cdot 0-2)+\sum_{R\in C}(e_R-1),
\]

with \(g=1\) and \(d=2\),

\[
-2 = -4 + \sum_{R}(e_R-1)\;\Longrightarrow\;
\sum_{R}(e_R-1)=2 .
\]

Thus the total ramification contribution is \(2\).  
Each simple ramification point contributes \(e_R-1 = 1\); therefore \(\pi\) has exactly two ramification points.

A ramification point \(R\) means that the line \(PR\) is tangent to \(C\) at \(R\).

* the tangent line to \(C\) at \(P\) itself, and  
* one further line through \(P\) tangent to \(C\) at a different point.
